Apple has filed documents regarding the App Store external transaction commission issue in the Epic Games lawsuit. Below are the relevant details.

Apple submits proposal on App Store external transaction commission

After multiple requests to stay the district court proceedings—which will determine how and whether Apple can charge commissions on transactions conducted within the App Store but outside its IAP system—Apple has finally submitted its proposal, outlining the suggested fee structure.

Apple submitted this proposal shortly after the Supreme Court denied its request to stay the lower court proceedings. Apple had hoped to stay the relevant proceedings so the Supreme Court could hear its case; had things gone its way, Apple could have been found in contempt of court for charging a 27% commission on App Store external transactions. Earlier, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers had issued an injunction requiring Apple to allow developers to direct users to other purchasing methods.

Apple argued both at the district court level and subsequently before the Supreme Court that the court's ruling could affect the outcome of the fee determination proceedings, and that the relevant proceedings should therefore be stayed pending the court's decision. However, the Supreme Court denied Apple's request, allowing the district court proceedings to continue during the trial.

Accordingly, Apple has now submitted its proposal, with the suggested fees as follows:

Standard apps charged 15% (such apps currently pay a 30% in-app purchase ("IAP") commission);

Apple stated: "Factual and expert evidence regarding the above-suggested commission rates has also been submitted concurrently." The company further added:

Apple further noted that its "suggested external link commission can also be compared with the commissions of other competing app stores," including Google Play, Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

The company also mentioned: "The standard external link fee structure for the Google Play Store is: standard rate 20%, program rate 15%, subscription rate 10%—these rates are also agreed upon by Epic."

Apple stated it still believes the fee determination proceedings should be stayed pending the outcome of the Supreme Court case, and added that submitting this proposal is purely in compliance with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's instructions.

The company also pointed out that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's blanket injunction on external link transaction commissions, and stated that the relevant commissions would only be problematic if they effectively constituted a de facto prohibition.

Following Apple's submission, Epic can now respond, and Apple is expected to submit its brief to the Supreme Court before September 14.
